title: Cost-Benefit Optimality of Gene Expression
markdown: ## What this covers Can a protein's expression level be explained as the outcome of natural selection balancing a cost against a benefit? This chapter works through Dekel and Alon's 2005 study of the *lac* operon as a test case, following the lecture's path: how cost and benefit were each measured, what the data can and cannot support, and what a laboratory evolution experiment showed when set against the resulting predictions. Along the way the lecture takes a long detour into how to read an error bar and how many fitting parameters a curve is allowed before its fit stops meaning anything — a detour that turns out to be exactly what is needed to judge the paper's central claim. The chapter assumes the basic *lac* operon circuitry (*lacZ*, *lacY*, the repressor, IPTG as a gratuitous inducer) and enough statistics to know what a standard deviation is. ## The optimization question Different proteins are expressed at different levels, and one broad explanatory stance is that a given level evolved, over some unknown ancestral history, to solve a cost–benefit problem: making the protein costs the cell resources it could have spent elsewhere, and not making it forfeits whatever the protein does for the cell. Dekel and Alon's paper on the *lac* operon is a clean attempt to make that story quantitative for one system, and the lecture treats it as a case study in how far you can push an optimization argument on real data — including where the argument turns out to be weaker than the paper's framing suggests. A single convincing case would not show that *every* protein's level is optimized; it would only show that the story is coherent for this one. To ask about cost and benefit for the *lac* system, recall what the operon actually buys the cell: **LacY** is a membrane transporter that actively imports lactose, and **LacZ** (β-galactosidase) cleaves the imported lactose — a disaccharide — into its two monosaccharides, which the rest of the cell's existing metabolism can then use. (The operon's third gene, *lacA*, does not enter the discussion.) The cost is that building LacY and LacZ consumes resources the cell could otherwise have put into proteins it does use; the benefit, when lactose is around, is the sugar those two proteins let the cell eat. ## Measuring cost To isolate the cost from the benefit, the experiment has to titrate the level of *lac* expression **without** any lactose present, so that the operon is being paid for but not used. This is done with **IPTG**, a gratuitous inducer that relieves the repressor's inhibition of the *lac* promoter without itself being a substrate, so its concentration can be dialled to set the expression level anywhere between zero and full induction. The cells are grown on a low concentration of glycerol as a second-rate carbon source — some carbon source has to be provided or nothing grows, but glycerol alone doesn't create a benefit that would confound the measurement of cost. The measured quantity is **relative growth rate reduction**: the percentage decrease in growth rate relative to a strain with no *lac* induction, plotted against expression level relative to full induction of the wild type. The result is a cost curve that grows faster than linearly (convex — positive second derivative) in expression, reaching roughly a **4% growth-rate deficit at full induction**, with data points around relative expression 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 (expression above 1 isn't reachable with the wild-type promoter and no lactose feedback; a stronger promoter could in principle push past it). Superlinear cost is one of the paper's central quantitative claims, and it deserves scrutiny before moving on — which is exactly what the lecture does next, by way of a general question about how to read noisy data. ## Reading a fitted curve: how many error bars should miss it? Suppose you measure some true, "god-given" relationship $y(x)$ at several values of $x$, each measurement corrupted by Gaussian noise, and you plot the mean and the standard error at each $x$. What fraction of those error bars should actually contain the true curve? The **standard error of the mean** answers a different question from the **standard deviation**. The standard deviation describes how spread out individual measurements are — it is a statement about how good the experimentalist's instrument is. What the experimenter actually wants to know is the *mean* of the underlying distribution — the true growth-rate deficit at that expression level — and that is a much sharper quantity once you average over repeated measurements. If you sample $n$ times from a distribution with standard deviation $\sigma$ and average, the distribution of that mean is (by the central limit theorem, regardless of the shape of the original noise) itself approximately Gaussian, centred on the true value, with width $$\text{SEM} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.$$ In the paper, each point comes from 48 independently grown cultures arranged in a checkerboard pattern on a microtiter plate, and the plotted error bars are the standard error of that mean, not the raw standard deviation of the 48 growth-rate measurements (which the lecture notes is itself around 3–4%, i.e. comparable to or larger than the 4% effect being measured). Now the question: a $\pm 1\sigma$ error bar around a Gaussian-distributed sample mean misses the true mean about a third of the time by construction. So **roughly a third of your error bars should fail to touch the true curve** — and this fraction is essentially independent of $n$. Increasing $n$ shrinks each error bar (by $\sqrt n$), but it *also* pulls each sample mean closer to the true value by the same factor, so the two effects cancel and the fraction of misses stays put. There is a common instinct to be suspicious of a model, or a measurement, whenever an error bar doesn't touch the fitted curve — the correct reaction is the opposite: if *every* error bar touches the curve, something is off. ## Overfitting: parameters are not free The lecture then asks the same question with a twist: what if the curve being compared to the data isn't the true underlying relationship, but a curve **fit** to the data using some number of free parameters? Does the same "about a third should miss" rule still hold? It does not, and the reason is worth having explicit. If you have $n$ measured points and use $n$ free parameters, you are no longer really fitting anything — you are solving a system of equations, and the resulting curve passes through **every** data point exactly, error bars included, regardless of whether the underlying model has any truth to it. Fifteen data points and a 14-degree polynomial with fifteen free parameters will hit all fifteen points squarely, with no exceptions. This is not a mark of a good model; it is a mark of having used up all your degrees of freedom. The general warning: never let the number of fitting parameters get close to the number of data points, and expect a *reasonable* model — one with meaningfully fewer parameters than data points — to still miss some error bars. This bears directly on comparing the paper's candidate cost functions. A quadratic will always fit the cost data at least as well as a line, because a line is a special case of a quadratic — adding a parameter can only help the fit, whether or not the extra curvature is real. The question is not "does the quadratic fit better" (it must) but "can the data actually **reject** the simpler, linear model" — and the lecture's judgement is that they can reject it only weakly: eyeballing the four cost points, a straight line through them is not obviously bad. ## Two non-linear cost functions, and why the difference matters later The paper actually plots three curves against the cost data: a line, a quadratic, and a third curve — a model in which the cell has a finite pool of protein-making resources, and growth collapses to zero once expression exhausts it. Over the range where there is data, this "finite resources" curve and the plain quadratic are nearly indistinguishable — so close that no amount of data in that range could tell them apart, and the paper does not claim otherwise. The reason to carry two curves that agree everywhere you have data is that they disagree sharply **outside** that range, which matters for a prediction made later in the paper: given a benefit function and a cost function, where should a population evolve to under different lactose regimes? At high lactose concentrations, a quadratic cost (with no hard ceiling) would let a population evolve toward much higher expression — the lecture puts a number on it, roughly **five times** the wild-type level — while the finite-resources model caps expression near where it already is. The population's actual evolved expression level, plotted against the lactose concentration it evolved in, tracks the finite-resources curve and not the plain quadratic (or the line). This is presented in the paper as support for the finite-resources model specifically — though the lecture flags a loophole: the wild-type promoter itself cannot be induced past "1" without a mutation that strengthens it, so a population that has not yet found such a mutation in 500 generations would look capped near 1 regardless of which cost function is really operating. The evolution data are suggestive, not conclusive, for choosing between the non-linear models. ## Measuring benefit Measuring the benefit side means growing the cells with the *lac* operon fully induced (via IPTG, so expression is independent of lactose) across a range of **external lactose concentrations**, and again plotting relative growth rate. This is a proxy — plotting growth against lactose concentration rather than directly against benefit as a function of expression level, which would be the more direct quantity but is harder to control — and the paper's argument depends on that proxy being adequate. The resulting curve starts at roughly a 4–4.5% growth deficit with no lactose at all (this is just the cost of the induced, unused enzymes, matching the cost curve above), rises through zero, and saturates at a **growth advantage of around 10–11%** at high lactose. The saturation with lactose concentration is explained in the model by Michaelis–Menten import kinetics — import rate scaling as $[\text{lactose}]/(K + [\text{lactose}])$ — but that only explains saturation *as a function of lactose concentration*. It says nothing about whether benefit saturates as a function of the *amount of LacY made*, since more transporter could in principle keep raising the import rate even as any fixed amount of lactose saturates it. So this experiment does not actually rule out a benefit function that keeps rising, less than linearly, as expression increases — which turns out to be the important loose end. ## The laboratory evolution experiment The paper's most direct test is to let bacterial populations evolve for **500 generations** at several fixed lactose concentrations and ask what level of *lac* expression each population settles on. A few points about how this was actually run are worth having, because they generalize beyond this experiment: it is worth developing a habit of asking, for any experiment you read about, how long it must actually have taken. *E. coli* can divide roughly every 20 minutes in rich media — about 75 generations a day — which would put 500 generations within a week or two. That is not what happened, because the experiment used **daily batch culture with a 100-fold dilution** each day, which works out to only about **6.6 generations per day**: cells transferred into fresh medium sit for an hour or two before dividing, then grow exponentially for some hours, then saturate and sit at that density for the rest of the day until the next dilution. Getting to 500 generations this way took roughly **three months**. Under IPTG (so expression is decoupled from lactose), the evolved, normalized LacZ activity moved in the expected direction with the lactose concentration the population evolved in: essentially unchanged at a moderate concentration, decreased in populations evolved with no lactose at all, and increased in populations evolved at higher lactose. Across all of the lactose concentrations tested, though, no evolved population pushed normalized expression much past about **1.2–1.3 times** the wild-type level — a real constraint against expression climbing without bound, consistent with *some* nonlinearity limiting the benefit of ever more expression, whichever specific cost or benefit function is responsible. A separate control makes the logic of cost sharper. Populations evolved **without IPTG and without lactose** for 500 generations — so the operon was never expressed and never paid for — lost the ability to grow on lactose altogether: roughly a kilobase spanning the promoter was deleted from the genome. The lecture's point is about *why* that mutant could spread: with the operon not being expressed, there was essentially no cost differential left to select on (only the marginal cost of replicating that stretch of DNA), so a mutant that happened to delete it had almost nothing to gain — and yet it still swept the population. That sets up the next lecture's topic, neutral evolution, as the right lens for mutations with little or no selective advantage. ## Is the cost really super-linear? A complication from later work The lecture flags that subsequent measurements complicate the paper's central quantitative claim. Terry Hwa's group has since characterized growth-rate cost as a function of expressing a variety of non-useful proteins (including β-galactosidase and β-lactamase) and finds it looks essentially **linear**, saturating only much further out — around 30% of total cellular protein — than the range relevant here. If cost really is linear rather than super-linear, the finite-resources story loses its footing, and it also raises a conceptual problem: overall growth is (something like) benefit minus cost, and if *both* cost and benefit were straight lines in expression, their difference would be a straight line too, with **no interior optimum at all**. The lecture's own guess, offered explicitly as a guess rather than something the paper establishes, is that the relevant non-linearity sits on the **benefit** side rather than the cost side: benefit should be sub-linear in expression, for much the same reason the first slice of pizza is worth more than the fifth — beyond some point, more transporter and more enzyme just aren't as useful, whether because the cell has enough sugar already or because the efficiency of using it changes with supply. Since all of the candidate cost functions behave alike over the range where there is data, none of the paper's predictions in that range are actually very sensitive to which cost function is used — the sensitivity, and the disagreement with later work, is specifically about what happens *outside* the measured range, which is exactly where extrapolation is least trustworthy. ## What else might be under selection The framework so far assumes growth rate — the rate of division — is the thing evolution is optimizing during the lab evolution experiment. The lecture pauses to list other quantities a population might instead (or additionally) be optimizing over a daily batch-dilution cycle: - **Maximum density reached** before saturation. - **Rate of death during stationary phase** — cultures that die more slowly while saturated can spread even without dividing faster. This is the regime of *GASP* ("growth advantage in stationary phase") mutants, some of which gain their advantage by consuming the contents of cells that lyse around them. - **Length of the lag phase** at the start of each day — a mutant that starts dividing sooner after dilution gets a head start on spreading before its competitors even begin. These are flagged as real alternatives worth keeping in mind whenever "optimizing growth rate" is used as a modeling assumption, not as claims the lecture verifies for this particular experiment. ## What was *not* under selection here One category of mutation the evolution experiment did **not** see is worth noting on its own: no increase in LacZ's specific activity (enzymatic activity normalized by the amount of LacZ protein present). One reading is that the enzyme itself is already near-optimal, having been shaped by a much longer evolutionary history (plausibly in the gut, where *E. coli* actually meets lactose) than five hundred generations in the lab could improve on. The lecture adds an explicit caveat: an enzyme tuned to a different environment (gut pH and conditions) than the lab's could in principle still have room to adapt to the lab — so "we didn't see improvement" is consistent with prior optimization but does not prove it. ## Sources - Transcript: `recordings/9ygxpwvwydy.md` (MIT 8.591J, Fall 2014), the full lecture. - Framing of the optimization question and the *lac* operon components — 00:00–09:11. - Cost measurement design (IPTG, no lactose, glycerol) and the cost curve — 09:11–17:15. - Standard error of the mean, the central-limit-theorem argument, and the fraction of error bars expected to miss the true curve — 17:15–32:05. - Overfitting and the number-of-parameters argument, applied back to the cost-function fits — 32:05–44:32. - The two non-linear cost functions and why they can't be distinguished from the cost data alone — 43:28–49:13. - Later data on whether cost is really super-linear (Terry Hwa's group) and the case for the non-linearity being on the benefit side — 49:13–57:11. - Benefit measurement (lactose titration) and Michaelis–Menten import kinetics — 57:11–1:01:57. - Laboratory evolution experiment: design, timing, daily batch dilution — 1:01:57–1:09:58. - What else might be optimized (GASP mutants, lag time, Lenski's long-term evolution experiment) — 1:08:47–1:13:21. - Evolved expression results, the no-IPTG control and the operon deletion, and closing remarks — 1:13:21–1:19:29. - Referred to but not contained in the transcript: Dekel, E. and Alon, U., "Optimality and evolutionary tuning of the expression level of a protein," *Nature* 436 (2005) — the paper under discussion; the lecture assumes the class read it beforehand. Also referred to: unpublished/later phenomenological growth-law work from Terry Hwa's group on the cost of non-useful protein expression, and Richard Lenski's long-term *E. coli* evolution experiment at Michigan State — neither is otherwise described in this transcript.
